The governing idea

Premium does not mean less information. It means less effort to decide.

Apple-like restraint created desire, but a high-value purchase in Vietnam still depended on price, promotion, variants, installments, trade-in, availability, delivery and warranty.

01Keep the product and its value proposition in visual control.
02Surface decision information when its question becomes active.
03Use progressive disclosure to preserve context—not to hide complexity.
04Adopt familiar commerce patterns selectively, with premium hierarchy.

My remit

Three layers of the same problem.

As Senior Product Designer, I connected user feedback, commercial priorities and interaction decisions. The work was not a set of isolated screens; each workstream made the next one more coherent.

Experience

Home, Category and PLP

Audited hierarchy and reframed discovery around the decisions shoppers needed to make before considering a product.

Conversion

Checkout journey

Translated user feedback into hypotheses, redesigned friction points and evaluated the outcome through checkout completion.

System

Web and mobile behavior

Standardized reusable components, states and interaction rules so the experience could stay predictable as it scaled.

Brand-first

Desire through focus

  • Minimal and editorial
  • Strong product photography
  • Launch and campaign storytelling
  • Consistent premium perception

Risk: a beautiful showroom that shoppers leave to compare elsewhere.

Commerce-first

Confidence through facts

  • Visible price and promotions
  • Variant and product comparison
  • Availability and fulfillment
  • Fast, predictable purchase

Risk: an interchangeable discount retailer with weakened brand equity.

Diagnosis

The pages worked. The journey did not yet think as one.

The right information existed, but page-by-page priorities forced shoppers to rebuild context as they moved toward checkout.

01

Why did checkout feel difficult?

Product, price and purchase questions were still being resolved while the transaction was already in progress.

02

Why were questions unresolved?

Home, Category, PLP and Checkout evolved as separate surfaces with different priorities.

03

Why were priorities inconsistent?

Brand, merchandising, conversion and platform consistency were treated as separate delivery goals.

04

Why did the experience fragment?

No shared rule defined which information should lead, persist or remain secondary at each decision.

05

Why was there no shared rule?

Success was framed around pages and campaigns, not the shopper’s end-to-end ability to choose and complete.

Root cause

Fragmented journey ownership—and no shared decision architecture or component behavior model across web and mobile.

The redesign model

Four gates. One continuous purchase decision.

Each surface was assigned one primary job, so complexity arrived in the order shoppers could use it.

OrientWhere do I start?
NarrowWhich option fits?
DecideIs this right?
CompleteCan I finish?
01Orient / Home

Turn the home page into a compass.

Shopper question: “Where should I start?”

Home needed to connect product desire with a clear next step. Product families and major purchase paths should lead; broad promotion should support them.

  • Lead with product families and launches.
  • Separate product-led from promotion-led modules.
  • Reduce competition between campaigns and entry points.
  • Preserve a direct path into the relevant category.
02Narrow / Category + PLP

Make promotion calculable, not loud.

Shopper question: “Which products are worth considering?”

Listings needed enough information to remove unviable options without turning every card into a campaign poster.

  • Group products by meaningful differences.
  • Keep price visible across comparable items.
  • Use filters tied to actual category decisions.
  • Let promotion support—not replace—product identity.
01Payable priceLead
02Primary offerSupport
03ConditionsOn demand
04Trust signalNear action
03Decide / PDP

Stage the questions before the buy button.

Shopper question: “Is this the right product and offer?”

The product detail page became the decision environment: product → variant → price → offer → fulfillment → confidence.

  • Keep the selected configuration visible.
  • Reveal the real payable price and offer hierarchy.
  • Connect availability to the selected variant.
  • Place delivery and warranty near commitment.

04 / Complete

+13%

uplift in checkout conversion following the redesigned checkout journey.

The proof story

  1. 01

    User feedback

    Signals identified effort, unclear states and confidence gaps in the transaction.

  2. 02

    Testable hypotheses

    Changes targeted effort, clarity and confidence—not subjective visual preference.

  3. 03

    Design response

    Action order, purchase summary, required information, validation and recovery became more predictable.

  4. 04

    Behavioral outcome

    Checkout completion improved by 13% after the redesigned journey.

Evidence boundary: 13% is a relative uplift in checkout conversion—not 13 percentage points and not an outcome attributed to every ShopDunk initiative. Baseline, denominator and experiment setup are not included in the public case.

System layer

A Design System is a behavior contract—not a component shelf.

The system translated the decision architecture into repeatable rules across web and mobile.

Layer 01

Foundations

Type, spacing, color, grid, radius and emphasis establish a shared visual grammar.

Layer 02

Components

Product cards, selectors, actions, inputs, feedback and summaries include states and behavior.

Layer 03

Patterns

Discovery, configuration, promotion, validation and checkout rules keep decisions consistent.

Example behavior model

Availability is a decision state.

In stockPrimary purchase action available.
Limited stockUrgency shown without overwhelming the product.
Variant unavailableSelection retained; recovery options offered.
Out of stockPurchase action replaced by availability recovery.
Store onlyOnline intent transfers to store selection.

Senior operating model

Designing across the seams.

Product + DesignTurn journey questions into shared priorities and testable hypotheses.
Marketing + CommerceGive launches and promotions defined hierarchy instead of competing for every surface.
EngineeringAlign reusable behavior, responsive states and handoff rules before implementation.
OperationsKeep availability, delivery and store handoff understandable at the moment of commitment.

Impact and reflection

The redesign changed the unit of design—from pages to decisions.

01 / CONVERSION

Measurable checkout improvement

13% uplift tied specifically to the redesigned checkout journey.

02 / JOURNEY

One connected decision model

Home, Category, PLP, PDP and Checkout each resolve a distinct shopper question.

03 / SYSTEM

More predictable behavior

Shared components include states, validation, feedback and usage rules across platforms.

04 / PRACTICE

Hypotheses over opinions

User feedback becomes testable design change with a behavioral success measure.

Good UX does not remove complexity. It decides where complexity belongs.

For ShopDunk, decision clarity became the premium experience.
